name: Cedarwood

lead: Cedarwood is the wood oil distilled from conifers commonly called cedars, though most commercial oil comes from junipers and cypresses. It supplies a dry, woody note in perfumery and appears in beard oils, soaps and colognes, so its main appearance payoff is scent as part of grooming.

Its main components are sesquiterpenes such as cedrol and cedrene. Research includes fragrance chemistry, toxicology and one randomized aromatherapy trial for alopecia areata in which cedarwood was one of four oils.

paras: People meet cedarwood as a note in colognes, as an ingredient in beard oils, soaps and hair products, or as a diluted essential oil in scalp massage blends. Scent-focused users choose it for a dry, woody character.

Dermal toxicity studies in rodents and the general guidance on essential oils indicate skin irritation or allergy is possible; products are normally diluted. Regulators such as the US EPA describe registered cedarwood products as low risk when used as directed.

chain: Wood oil distilled from cedar-type trees
Added to colognes, beard oils and soaps
Dry woody scent as part of grooming
angle.text: Cedarwood adds a dry, woody scent to fragrance and grooming products. In scalp blends it is used alongside other oils, which is where its hair connection comes from.

lead: Cedarwood refers to essential oils distilled from the wood of trees called cedar, including true cedars (Cedrus) and junipers, cypresses and thujas that share the common name. The oils are dominated by sesquiterpenes such as cedrenes, cedrol and thujopsene, which give the characteristic dry woody scent [1][2].

In appearance terms its role is olfactory: it is a base note in colognes and a component of grooming products such as beard oils and soaps. Perfumers also synthesise woody and ambery materials from cedrene [3].

Research includes a 1998 randomized trial in 86 people with alopecia areata where a daily scalp massage with a blend of thyme, rosemary, lavender and cedarwood oils was compared with carrier oils alone; 44 percent of the active group improved versus 15 percent of controls [4].
infobox: Considered low risk by the US EPA when used as directed

paras: Cedarwood oil serves as a woody note in fragrance, soaps and men's grooming blends. Fragrance chemistry reviews describe cedarwood-derived compounds such as alpha-cedrene as starting points for woody and ambery perfumery ingredients [1][3].

Cedarwood was one of four essential oils in the alopecia areata trial published in Archives of Dermatology, applied in jojoba and grapeseed carrier oils for seven months. Blinded photograph assessment found more improvement in the oil group [4]. A later scoping review of essential oils for inflammatory skin conditions found tea tree oil was the most studied oil; cedarwood was not the focus [5].
A 2026 review notes that oils from true cedars are rich in himachalenes and atlantones, while Juniperus virginiana and related oils are rich in cedrenes, cedrol and thujopsene [2].
The US National Toxicology Program published dermal toxicity studies of Virginia cedarwood oil in rats and mice [6]. Essential oils in general can cause contact reactions in some people [5].

One randomized, double-blind trial included cedarwood in a four-oil blend for alopecia areata, finding improvement in 44 percent of the active group versus 15 percent of controls; the effect of cedarwood alone was not separated [4]. Other studies listed for cedarwood concern chemistry, mouse obesity models and laboratory methods and are not human appearance trials.
Cedarwood oil has been used since antiquity, including in Egyptian embalming and as a microscopy immersion oil until synthetic substitutes appeared in the 1940s [7].
